author: David Luu
headline: Smartwatch AI matched office cuffs at flagging hypertension
text: An AI model reading the optical and motion sensors in a consumer smartwatch identified adults with hypertension about as accurately as an initial office blood pressure check, Google Research and colleagues at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School reported in Nature on November 5. Why it matters: More than half of adults with high blood pressure do not know they have it, and a cuff reading only happens when someone is in a clinic. A watch that flags a likely hypertensive state from days of passive data could send people to get a proper cuff measurement. The model does not estimate a blood pressure number and needs no cuff calibration, which is where most wrist blood pressure attempts have failed. What the study found: Design: prospective, multicenter study at five U.S. sites in 196 adults with no known cardiovascular disease and not on blood pressure medication, with 24-hour ambulatory monitoring as the reference standard and seven days of watch wear. Model: a neural network pretrained on 492,347 hours of unlabeled sensor data from 2,109 people, reading 15-second windows of photoplethysmography and accelerometry, with the accelerometer capturing the ballistocardiogram. Day-level outputs plus height feed a logistic regression that returns a probability score. Screening: sensitivity 65.8% (95% CI 54.0 to 76.3) and specificity 90.0% (95% CI 83.2 to 94.7), positive predictive value 80.6%. A single office reading in the same people gave 55.3% sensitivity at the same 90.0% specificity. Confirmation: in the 48 participants with an elevated initial office reading, the watch reached 78.4% sensitivity and 90.9% specificity, against 67.6% and 63.6% for a repeat office reading. Multi-day home cuff monitoring did better on sensitivity, at 89.2%. Signal: higher-risk waveforms showed narrower pulses, slower systolic upstroke and wider motion complexes, which the authors read as stiffer arteries and altered cardiac mechanics. Limitations: The watch missed about a third of people with hypertension on ambulatory monitoring, so a negative result tells a patient little. The study enrolled 196 people at five sites, excluded anyone with known cardiovascular disease or on antihypertensive drugs, and the paper is behind a paywall, so the full demographic breakdown and the hypertension threshold used are not in the open text. Google employs the lead authors and the work informed a feature in its own app. The authors state this is early feasibility research, not a replacement for a cuff, not a diagnosis and not an approved device. No regulatory clearance is described. For longevitydocs: Patients already arrive with watch data, and this adds a category that looks clinical. The honest framing for them is that a positive flag is a reason to book a proper measurement, and a negative one changes nothing. Nothing here replaces an ambulatory monitor, which remains the test that settles the question when office readings disagree. What makes this worth tracking is the comparison the authors chose: a single clinic reading is a weaker screen than most patients assume, and that is the bar being cleared. Originally published in The Longevity Medicine Newsletter, Dr. David Luu's Sunday newsletter. Sources: Di Achille P, Poh M-Z, et al.
